planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, in hills spaced widely to allow the sprawling vines room to run.

directions: Delica is the dark green, deeply lobed kabocha type most widely sold as fresh kabocha in North American grocery stores, prized for its dry, deep-orange flesh with a dense, chestnut-like sweetness. Vines are vigorous and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit set, tapering off as the rind hardens near harvest. Cure fruit for one to two weeks in a warm spot to concentrate sugars before moving to cool storage, where it keeps for two to three months. Choose Delica when you want the classic Japanese squash experience for tempura, soups, and roasting rather than a sweeter American-bred kabocha hybrid.

planting.note: Sow directly into warm, fertile hills once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F, well after last frost.

directions: Golden Delicious is a 1920s Oregon-bred heirloom, a cross of Delicious and Boston Marrow, grown for its top-shaped, red-orange fruit and thick, fine-grained flesh originally favored for commercial baby food production. Give the long vines plenty of room and consistent moisture through fruit development, then let fruit finish on the vine until the rind resists a thumbnail. It stores exceptionally well for a maxima squash, often holding good eating quality into winter without special curing conditions. Gardeners choose it today for its old-fashioned sweetness in pies and its reliability as a dependable keeper compared to showier modern hybrids.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills of compost-enriched soil after all danger of frost, spacing hills widely for the vigorous vines.

directions: Australian Butter is an uncommon heirloom maxima squash producing large, pale peach-orange fruit with a hard rind and dry, deep-orange flesh that bakes up dense and sweet. It needs a long, warm season and generous spacing since a single vine can cover significant ground while setting several 15-pound fruits. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to die back, then cure in a warm, airy location for one to two weeks before storing. It appeals to gardeners hunting for lesser-known maxima types with outstanding dessert-quality flesh and long winter storage life.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season climates and transplant out once soil has warmed.

directions: Autumn Crown is a modern interspecific F1 hybrid bred by crossing a Crown Prince-type maxima with a butternut moschata to combine butternut's sweet, dense flesh with earlier ripening and better cool-weather set. Its more compact vines and shorter days to maturity make it a good option for gardeners in cooler or shorter-season regions where standard butternuts often fail to fully ripen. Fruit develops a classic buff-tan skin and a small seed cavity, giving high usable flesh yield per squash. Grow it as you would any butternut, but expect a slightly earlier harvest window and more reliable ripening under marginal heat conditions.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; the compact bush habit suits smaller gardens and tighter row spacing than vining acorn types.

directions: Sweet REBA (Resistant Early Bush Acorn) is a Cornell University release bred for a truly compact, non-vining bush habit combined with earliness and improved powdery mildew tolerance, making it well suited to short-season and small-space gardens. Despite its small footprint, plants set heavy yields of dark green, ribbed, one-to-one-and-a-half-pound fruit with notably sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh. Its bush form allows closer in-row spacing than sprawling acorn varieties, so it fits well in raised beds or intensive plantings. Choose Sweet REBA when garden space is limited but you still want reliably sweet, early-maturing acorn squash for fall roasting.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
